content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a work on learning with noisy labels. The class-agnostic sample selection approach is improved through class prototypes. Based on a prior framework designed for handling noisy labels, extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method of this paper achieves competitive classification performance on multiple tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths** 
- Experimental results are abundant, which shows that the proposed method is a state-of-the-art one.

**Weaknesses**
- The contribution of this paper is overclaimed. Besides, the technical contribution is weak.
- Theoretical analysis is not convincing and likely to be problematic. 
- Writing needs to be improved. It is hard to follow the implementation of the method. Also, lots of claims/explanations/descriptions are confusing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity & Quality**   
There are many unclear explanations in this paper. The quality is not satisfactory. Specifically,   
- The paper overclaimed its contribution. It claims that "this paper first reveal this long-ignored problem". It is not true. Prior works [R1] (see its Figure 1) actually have discussed the difference of multiple classes about data memorization during training. 
- The class-agnostic issue is easy to understand. However, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test instead makes readers confused. 
- The paper argues that the GMM method for sample selection is class-agnostic, and therefore we improve it. However, this method is still involved in the proposed framework, which is a bit contradictory. Besides, if the errors brought by this GMM method are accumulated, the proposed framework will be influenced largely. 
- What is the relationship between the EM algorithm and used implementation? It seems that the paper uses Eq. (5) in optimization but does not use the EM algorithm. If so, why the theoretical analysis is conducted with EM? Besides, the theoretical analysis does not export a useful result. The paper only simply claims that the obtained loss values can be used effectively for sample selection, which is not rigorous for a theory. At least, the convergence of EM and results obtained after convergence should be provided.
- An algorithm flow could be provided to better follow the implementation of the framework.  
- One minor comment. Noisy labels are not incorrect labels. They consist of both clean and incorrect labels.

[R1] Yisen Wang et al. Symmetric Cross Entropy for Robust Learning with Noisy Labels. In ICCV, 2019.

**Novelty**  
The novelty of this paper is limited. The motivation of this paper is good, which targets the class-agnostic issue of existing sample selection methods. However, the framework implementation is a bit rough. It seems that the paper simply combines unsupervised learning methods and semi-supervised learning methods for handle noisy labels to improve the network robustness. Both conceptual and technical novelty cannot meet the requirements of a top-tier conference. 

**Reproducibility**   
The reproducibility of this paper may be not satisfactory. Although the paper provides some implementation details of the proposed framework, too many hyper-parameters are included and need to be determined. In fact, the DivideMix framework has contained many hyper-parameters, the proposed framework additionally introduces $\alpha$, $e$, and $\tau$. These hyper-parameters cannot be determined through standard machine learning paradigms such as (cross-) validation and grid search methods.  Therefore, the reproducibility may be not good enough. One suggestion is that the paper could provide all needed hyper-parameters and carefully discuss how to tune them in practice, i.e., only with training and validation sets.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper provides a complicated framework for learning with noisy labels. Although reported experimental results are promising, the paper should be improved to reach the acceptance of ICLR (see the explanations above). Therefore, this paper cannot be recommended for acceptance at the present stage.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 9dhn -- Part 1/2
content.comment:
Thanks for your careful review and thoughtful comments. We will  carefully update our paper with your advices. Now we address your comments as follows:

**Q1. The paper overclaimed its contribution. It claims that "this paper first reveal this long-ignored problem". It is not true. Prior works [1] (see its Figure 1) actually discussed the difference between multiple classes about data memorization during training.**

**A1.** We are sorry for the missing reference. [1] discussed the difference between multiple classes about data memorization during training and focused on the problem of significant under learning in hard classes caused by the issue.  In our paper, we also discuss the data memorization issue, but the key point of **our work focuses on another problem, i.e., class agnostic loss distribution modeling problem** caused by the issue. We actually claim that we reveal the class agnostic loss distribution modeling problem **in the context of label noise cleaner**. We will fix the inappropriate statements and discuss [1] in our paper to make our contribution more clear.

[1] Yisen Wang et al. Symmetric Cross Entropy for Robust Learning with Noisy Labels. In ICCV, 2019.

**Q2. The class-agnostic issue is easy to understand. However, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test instead makes readers confused.**

**A2.** Sorry for the unclear statement. We attempt to adopt KS test to reveal the issue quantitatively. We will make it more clear in our paper.

**Q3. The paper argues that the GMM method for sample selection is class-agnostic, and therefore we improve it. However, this method is still involved in the proposed framework, which is a bit contradictory.**

**A3.** We did not totally remove the GMM cleaner from our framework because (1) it introduces the "small loss prior" to help the learning of prototypes, and (2) ensures the stable work of the framework, giving the CPC enough time to warm up. The prototype quality comparisons between CPC and the conventional prototype learning method stated in section5.3 demonstrates that our method learns better prototypes.

To further demonstrate the contribution of the GMM cleaner, we  remove the GMM cleaner and learn class prototypes in CPC via the typical prototypical contrastive objective as in MoPro [2].In experiments, we find that without the help of the GMM cleaner, the learnt prototypes generate less accurate data partition that further drawing back the overall training framework for DNNs as shwon in Table1. The situation is especially severe on the challenging benchmark with more diverse data, _e.g.,_ WebVision. On WebVision, due to the weak performance of prototypes, only ~13% of total training data are classfied as clean data, where the number of true clean data would be even less, which greatly hinders the performance of the method. The results demonstrate the benefits of the GMM cleaner in our method. 

$~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~$ **Table1. Ablation study on the contribution of GMM cleaner.**
| method              | CIFAR-100(sym90%) | WebVision | CIFAR-10(asym40%) | Clothing1M |
|---------------------|-------------------|-----------|-------------------|------------|
| Baseline            | 41.2              | 76.3      | 94.6              | 74.73      |
| _CPC w/o GMM Cleaner_ | 42.9              | 26.8      | 93.92             | 74.09      |
| CPC                 | **54.6**              | **79.63**     | **94.73**             | **75.4**       | 

[2] Junnan Li, Caiming Xiong, and Steven CH Hoi. Mopro: Webly supervised learning with momentum prototypes. ICLR2021.

**Q4.If the errors brought by this GMM method are accumulated, the proposed framework will be influenced largely.**

**A4.** As analyzed in section 4.3, after CPC warm-upped, with the class-aware modulation by CPC, the probability distribution of clean or noise of a sample given by GMM cleaner , _i.e._, $q(z')$, would be gradually approximate to the one given by class-aware CPC _i.e.,_ $q(z)$.  The performance of CPC presented in Fig.3 further shows that the proposed framework does not suffer from the problems brought about by accumulated GMM errors and CPC finally converge as a better label noise cleaner than GMM cleaner.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 9dhn -- Part 2/2
content.comment:
**Q5. What is the relationship between the EM algorithm and used implementation? It seems that the paper uses Eq. (5) in optimization but does not use the EM algorithm. If so, why the theoretical analysis is conducted with EM? Besides, the theoretical analysis does not export a useful result. The paper only simply claims that the obtained loss values can be used effectively for sample selection, which is not rigorous for a theory. At least, the convergence of EM and results obtained after convergence should be provided.**

**A5.** Our implementation is essentially an approximation of the EM algorithm. As illustrated in Section 4.3, in order to introduce the “small-loss prior” to provide stronger and
more robust supervision signals to the learning of CPC, in the E-step, we estimate the probability distribution of clean or unclean of samples, denoted as $q(z'_i)$, via the GMM cleaner, which is an approximation to the $q(z_i)$ in Eq.(8). And consequently, we replace the q(zi) in Eq.(9) with $q(z'_i)$ and find the prototype C to minimize the bound, which makes the loss function $L_C$ in Eq.(5) an approximation to Eq.(9). The detailed analysis on the relationship between Eq.(5) and Eq.(9) is as follows.

Firstly, we replace the estimation of CPC $q(z_i)$ in Eq.(9) with the estimation of GMM cleaner $q(z'_i)$ which is a justified approximate to $q(z_i)$:

$C^{new} =  \arg\min_{C} -  \sum_{ D} \sum_{z_{i} \in \{0,1\}} q(z_i) \log  p(y_i|C,x_i)$

$~~~~~~~~ \approx \arg\min_{C} -   \sum_{ D} \sum_{z'_i \in \{0,1\}} q(z'_i) \log   p(y_i|C,x_i)$   

$~~~~~~~~= \arg\min_{C} -   \sum_{ D} \left [ q(z'_i = 0) \log p(y_i|C,x_i) + q(z'_i = 1)\log p(y_i|C,x_i) \right]~~~~$
(14)

 In Eq.(5), $q(z'_i)$ is quantified to 1 and 0 by the threshold $\tau$, which makes it a "hard" version to  Eq.(14). Specifically, the first term in Eq.(14) updates the prototypes $C$ to better align the samples, that classified as clean, with annotated class prototypes. It is equivalent with the effect of Eq.(5) to clean label of positive samples, where:

 $~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~l = \log(\mathrm{sigmoid}(v'_i c_k^\top)), k=y_i, z'_i=0~~~~~~~$      (15)     

 where $v'_i$ is the embedding of sample $x_i$.
 The second term in Eq.(14) updates $C$ to prevent the samples, that classified as noise, from aligning with annotated class prototypes so as to better recognize the sample as noise (_i.e.,_ $z'_i=1$}), which is equivalent with the effect of Eq.(5) reducing the probability of negative samples being recognized as clean:
 
 $~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~l = \log(1-\mathrm{sigmoid}(v'_i c_k^\top)), k=y_i, z'_i=1~~~~~~~~$(16)
 
Thanks to the EM algorithm, it guarantees that our method will converge to a data partition effectively dividing clean and noise data, and consequently acts as a good label noise cleaner.

**Q6. An algorithm flow could be provided to better follow the implementation of the framework.**

**A6.** Thanks for your advice and we will provide the algorithm to the appendix of the revision of paper.

**Q7. These hyper-parameters cannot be determined through standard machine learning paradigms such as (cross-) validation and grid search methods. Therefore, the reproducibility may be not good enough. One suggestion is that the paper could provide all needed hyper-parameters and carefully discuss how to tune them in practice, i.e., only with training and validation sets.**

**A7.** In practical, if a clean validation set is accessible, we can determine the hyper-parameters by grid search. As for the hyper-parameter tunning in this paper, we mainly follow the tuning procedure introduced by DivideMix. First of all, we initialize the hyper-parameters to $e$=5%, $\tau$=0.5, $\alpha$=1. Then,  for the large scale real world benchmark Clothing1M and WebVision, the hyper-parameter tuning is done on the validation set of Clothing1M and transferred to WebVision. For CIFAR,  a small validation set with clean data is split from training data for hyperparameter tuning. Due to the diversity of experimental set-ups, it would be an irritating task to tune hyper-parameters for each experimental set-up respectively. Therefore, we only tune the hyperparameters under CIFAR-100(sym80%) and CIFAR-100(sym50%), and transfer the hyperparameters obtained  under CIFAR-100(sym80%) to the noisier set-up _i.e.,_ CIFAR-100(sym90%), and those obtained under CIFAR-100(sym50%) to the less challenge set-ups _i.e.,_ noise ratio lower than 50%  and all noise ratio on CIFAR-10.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a method for **label cleaning** based on a **prototype** classifier and combined it with **DivideMix** for learning from **noisy labels**. 
The method was evaluated on semi-synthetic datasets based on CIFAR-10/100, Clothing1M, and WebVision.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Class-dependent data cleaning may be a good direction and is worth further investigation. The prototype-based mislabeled instance detection is somehow novel.

However, there are several weaknesses:

1. The author claim that "the performance of unsupervised contrastive objectives highly depends on the quality of representation learned by the encoder" and "GMM cleaner can provide stronger and more robust supervision signals". There are a few issues: First, the author seems to imply that "depending on the quality of representation" is a drawback, but there is no evidence that the "prototypical contrastive objective" does not depend on the quality of representation anymore. Second, the "strongness and robustness" metric in this context is unclear. Nevertheless, the author provided no support for this claim.

2. The author did not explain Eq. (4). Why is pseudo-label needed, and why is this average strategy used?

3. I think the experimental setting with 90% symmetric noise is not a good proxy for real-world noisy label problems for two reasons: (1) the overall noise rate can rarely be as high as 90% in applications; (2) it is unlikely that the noise is instance-independent, let alone symmetric. Therefore, accuracy in such a setting may be a suboptimal metric and misleading for practitioners.

4. Section 5.3 cannot be called "analysis". The author only says things like, "we did this experiment, and we observed this outperformed that, so this is better". However, the mechanism of the proposed method is still unclear.
For example, the author stated that the purpose of the results in Figure 3 is to "figure out *why* CPC brings such a significant performance improvement." Still, the author did not explain the reasons adequately and did not provide enough support.
Moreover, the author seems to equate the final classification accuracy with the quality of prototypes. It is insufficient because the prototype is only one component of the learning method, and other aspects may also influence the final classification results.

The author also made several rookie mistakes:

1. It seems that the author does not understand the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and p-values. Distribution does not have a p-value. A hypothesis test has a p-value. A p-value less than 0.05 does not mean the confidence that two distributions are different is higher than 95%. It means that the probability that two distributions are the same is less than 5%. Rejecting the null hypothesis does not mean supporting or refuting the alternative hypothesis.

2. The author misused the term *loss* to mean *risk*.

3. $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ usually denotes an inner product, not a distance.

4. It seems that minimizing Eq. (2) does not minimize/maximize the distances (however they are defined).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing and organization of this paper can be improved. The code (with questionable comments) provided by the author is poorly organized and painful to read, so I could not check if the implementation is consistent with what the author proposed in this paper. Therefore I did not check the reproducibility.

Other issues are listed below.

- Adjectives like "impressive" or "outstanding" are subjective, unquantifiable, and inappropriate in scientific writing.

- I do not think "noisy unlabeled set" is an appropriate term (Yes, I do not think its use in DivideMix is appropriate, either). Noisy data implies that the data is labeled.

- About Figure 1:
  - How was epoch 30 and 10 chosen? 
  - What distribution assumption was used here? PDF should be non-negative.
  - Clean = all correct. Noisy = correct + incorrect. Do you mean mislabeled examples here?

- The caption of tables can be revised. What metric was reported? How many trials? What does the boldface mean (any statistical test used?), and is the result statistically significant?
content.summary_of_the_review: The author proposed a somehow novel idea and conducted experiments to verify it, but I think the mistakes outweigh the strengths. A few claims were not well-supported by convincing explanations or empirical evidence.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer TTo4 -- Part 1/2
content.comment:
Thanks for your careful review and thoughtful comments. We will  carefully update our paper with your advices. Now we address your comments as follows:

**Q1. The author claim that "the performance of unsupervised contrastive objectives highly depends on the quality of representation learned by the encoder" and "GMM cleaner can provide stronger and more robust supervision signals". The author seems to imply that "depending on the quality of representation" is a drawback, but there is no evidence that the "prototypical contrastive objective" does not depend on the quality of representation anymore. Second, the "strongness and robustness" metric in this context is unclear. Nevertheless, the author provided no support for this claim.**

**A1.**  First of all, we did not imply that "depending on the quality of representation" is a drawback but try to emphasize the fact that the effectiveness of typical contrastive objectives highly depends on the quality of representation.  The "**stronger and more robust supervision signals**" refer to **a higher ratio of correct training labels assigning  samples to  right class prototypes**, which introduce less noises to prototypes forming a better label noise cleaner to boost model performance. The "stronger and more robust supervision signals" can be measured by the ratio of correct training labels to all labels.

In typical prototypical contrastive objective, the unsupervised training labels are determined by similarity between samples and prototypes. Comapred to it, we empirically find that GMM cleaner provides more accurate training labels for prototypes, especially in the early stage of training. For example, in CIFAR-10(asym-40%), the averaged accuracy of training labels from GMM cleaner is 9.7% higher during the CPC warming up perioed.

Here we first present an intuitive explanation of the phenomenon.  In the early stage of training, where the prototypes are still too weak, it is too challenging to correctly assign samples to right prototypes by measuring the similarity between samples and prototypes. Compared to that, it would be easier for the GMM cleaner to recognize clean labels via "small loss prior" and provide more accurate labels to facilitate the learning of prototypes.

To further demonstrate the contribution of the GMM cleaner, we  remove the GMM cleaner and learn class prototypes in CPC via the typical prototypical contrastive objective as in MoPro [1].In experiments, we find that without the help of the GMM cleaner, the learnt prototypes generate less accurate data partition that further drawing back the overall training framework for DNNs as shwon in Table1. The situation is especially severe on the challenging benchmark with more diverse data, _e.g.,_ WebVision. On WebVision, due to the weak performance of prototypes, only ~13% of total training data are classfied as clean data, where the number of true clean data would be even less, which greatly hinders the performance of the method.  The results demonstrate the benefits of the GMM cleaner in our method. 

$~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~$ **Table1. Ablation study on the contribution of GMM cleaner.**
| method              | CIFAR-100(sym90%) | WebVision | CIFAR-10(asym40%) | Clothing1M |
|---------------------|-------------------|-----------|-------------------|------------|
| Baseline            | 41.2              | 76.3      | 94.6              | 74.73      |
| _CPC w/o GMM Cleaner_ | 42.9              | 26.8      | 93.92             | 74.09      |
| CPC                 | **54.6**              | **79.63**     | **94.73**             | **75.4**       | 

[1] Junnan Li, Caiming Xiong, and Steven CH Hoi. Mopro: Webly supervised learning with momentum prototypes. ICLR2021.

**Q2. The author did not explain Eq. (4). Why is pseudo-label needed, and why is this average strategy used?**

**A2.** Equation 4 is to select parts of high confidence samples from the unlabeled set to update prototypes, where the threshold for each class is the averaged classification probability of those samples belonging to that class in the clean set. The pseudo-label is introduced for the convenience of presentation.

**Q3. I think the experimental setting with 90% symmetric noise is not a good proxy for real-world noisy label problems.**

**A3.** We employ the setting with 90% symmetric noise following previous work, so as to provide fair and comprehensive comparisons with other methods. Thanks for your comment and we will not highlight the performance improvement achieved by our method under this setting as a major contribution in the revision of paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer TTo4 -- Part 2/2
content.comment:
**Q4. Section 5.3 cannot be called "analysis".  The author only says things like, "we did this experiment, and we observed this outperformed that, so this is better". However, the mechanism of the proposed method is still unclear. For example, the author stated that the purpose of the results in Figure 3 is to "figure out why CPC brings such a significant performance improvement." Still, the author did not explain the reasons adequately and did not provide enough support.**

**A4.** In section5.3, we attempt to conduct systematic ablation study by modifying the label noise cleaner while keeping other components in the framework unchanged, which is effective for analyzing the contribution of CPC to the overall framework. Since the data partition quality of label noise cleaner is critical to the performance overall framework [2], in Fig.3, we provide the intermediate results, _i.e.,_ data partition results of different label noise cleaners to directly verify the effect of CPC.

[2] Filipe R Cordeiro, Ragav Sachdeva, Vasileios Belagiannis, Ian Reid, and Gustavo Carneiro. Longremix: Robust learning with high confidence samples in a noisy label environment. Pattern Recognition, pp. 109013, 2022.

**Q5. The author seems to equate the final classification accuracy with the quality of prototypes. It is insufficient because the prototype is only one component of the learning method, and other aspects may also influence the final classification results.**

**A5.** We did not equate the final classification accuracy of DNNs with the quality of prototypes, though we consider high quality prototypes would greatly improve the final classification accuracy by providing high quality data partition. In the last paragraph of section5.3, to prove that with the help of GMM cleaner, our method can learn better prototypes, we compare our prototypes to the prototypes learnt by Mopro. To evaluate the quality of prototypes directly, we utilize prototypes rather than the DNNs to classify test samples. Compared to MoPro, our method learns better prototypes.

To further prove the effectiveness of our method in learning prototypes, we conduct the ablation study as discussed in response to **Q1**. We will add the discussion to the revision of paper to better support our statement.

**Q6. Questions about Figure 1. How was epoch 30 and 10 chosen? What distribution assumption was used here? PDF should be non-negative.**

**A6.** Epoch 30 and 10 are exactly where DNNs warming up phase is done and the losses distribution modeling is about to performed  in DivideMix framework for CIFAR100 and CIFAR10 datasets respectively.  For per-sample losses, GMM is employed to fit the distribution; for clean-sample and incorrect-sample (i.e. noise-sample mentioned in our paper) losses, Gaussian distribution  are employed. In our paper, we simply present the 95% confidence interval by shadows to indicate the variation of loss distribution for each class neglecting the fact that PDF should be non-negative. We are sorry for the rookie mistake and will fix the figure by truncating the negative parts of shadows to 0.

**Q7. The rookie mistakes and other issues.**

**A7.** Thanks very much for pointing out the mistakes and sorry for the bad reading experience. We will fix all the mistakes and issues in the revision of paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a new method for learning Deep Neural Networks for image classification with label noise. It is based on a semi-supervised approach and a previously proposed framework called DivideMix that iterates between a label noise partitioning step where the dataset is divided into clean and noisy samples and a DNN training step that optimises the neural network parameters on the estimated partitioned dataset.
The proposed approach replaces the class-agnostic partitioning by a class-aware prototype-based noise cleaner that trains a projection in a contrastive way resulting in embeddings that help to distinguish between clean and noisy samples.
Experimental results show that the approach outperforms the state of the art on learning with symmetric and asymmetric label noise on standard image classification benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts:
- Original approach taking into account the difference of clean and noisy examples' loss distributions among different classes. 
- Good experimental results
 
Weaknesses:
- The description of the overall procedure is quite difficult to understand (Fig. 2, Sect. 4.1).
- A more detailed ablation study would have been desirable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is mostly clear and easy to follow. However, the description of the overall procedure could be explained a bit better.
Also, the justification and intuition of some design choices and/or hyperparameters are not given, e.g. the warm-up phase and the fact that both a GMM cleaner and CPC are used in the proposed approach.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper is well written and relatively clear. The main contributions are clearly stated and experimentally validated and compared to the state of the art.

**A2.** In our method, we propose learning class prototypes to construct a class-aware label noise cleaner, _i.e.,_ CPC. We also keep the GMM cleaner because it is able to benefit the learning of prototypes with "small loss prior" and make the framework work stably during the warm-up period of CPC.

To better evaluate the contribution of GMM cleaner in our framework, we further present ablation study results as in Table.1. For _CPC w/o GMM Cleaner_, we  remove the GMM cleaner and learn class prototypes in CPC with prototypical contrastive objective as in MoPro [1]. In experiments, we find that without the help of the GMM cleaner, the learnt prototypes generate less accurate data partition that further drawing back the overall training framework for DNNs as shwon in Table1. The situation is especially severe on the challenging benchmark with more diverse data, _e.g.,_ WebVision. On WebVision, due to the weak performance of prototypes, only ~13% of total training data are classfied as clean data, where the number of true clean data would be even less, which greatly hinders the performance of the method. The results demonstrate the benefits of the GMM cleaner in our method. 

$~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~$ **Table1. Ablation study on the contribution of GMM cleaner.**
| method              | CIFAR-100(sym90%) | WebVision | CIFAR-10(asym40%) | Clothing1M |
|---------------------|-------------------|-----------|-------------------|------------|
| Baseline            | 41.2              | 76.3      | 94.6              | 74.73      |
| _CPC w/o GMM Cleaner_ | 42.9              | 26.8      | 93.92             | 74.09      |
| CPC                 | **54.6**              | **79.63**     | **94.73**             | **75.4**       |

**Q3. The justification and intuition of some design choices and/or hyperparameters are not given, e.g. the warm-up phase.**

**A3.** For the choice of CPC warm-up phase (_i.e.,_ $e$) as well as other newly introduced hyperparameters, we mainly follow the tuning procedure as in DivideMix. First of all, we initialize the hyper-parameters to $e$=5%, $\tau$=0.5, $\alpha$=1. Then,  for the large scale real world benchmark Clothing1M and WebVision, the hyperparameter tuning is done on the validation set of Clothing1M and transferred to WebVision. For CIFAR,  a small validation set with clean data is split from training data for hyperparameter tuning. Due to the diversity of experimental set-ups, it would be an irritating task to tune hyperparameters for each experimental set-up respectively. content.title: Further clarification of the difference between our work and the prior work.
content.comment:
Thanks for your response.  We would like to emphasize that  though [R1] and our work observe similar phenomena, i.e., the DNN model would have different fitting speeds to data in different classes in deep learning, we solve different problems, and develop different techniques. Speciffically,

(1) we focus on a **totally different problem** raised by the phenomenon.  In [R1], they focus on the **effect of CE loss as a training objective** in label noise learning.  In our method, we focus on the **effect of sample loss as the indicator for label noise recognition**. In this paper, we are **the first to reveal that the assumption** that "the same loss value on samples in different categories can reflect the same degree of noise likelihood" **does not hold in practice** due to the "different fitting speeds to different classes" phenomenon. Through experimental study, we prove that  the class-agnositic loss modeling would result in sub-optimal label noise cleaner that partions data noise less accurately, and consequently hinder the performance of DNNs in label noise learning. The problem is **completely beyond the scope of [R1]**.

(2) We utilize a **totally different method** for label noise learning. **In [R1], they improve label noise learning by improving the training objective**. They present a symmeric cross entropy by introducing an extra noise tolerant term to CE loss to facilitate learning of hard classes. **In our method, we improve the training data quality to improve label noise learning.** We propose replacing the sample loss based label noise cleaner with a class-prototypes based cleaner, which partitions data noise more accurately. With better data partitions as training input, our method advances the performance of DNNs in label noise learning.
Moreover, our method outperforms [R1] by a large margin across all benchmarks.

content.title: Response to the related work [R2]
content.comment:
Thanks for your kind notification. [R2] propose learning class-prototypes with a clustering and selection strategy, and utilize the selected prototypes to generate pseudo-labels for the training of DNNs. The total framework works in an iterative manner, where the quality of prototypes and the performance of DNNs are mutully improved.

Our method is different from [R2] in 3 folds:

(1) **Different framework and motivation**. [R2] follows a label correction framework[R3,R4], which  is very similar to the MoPro[R3] that has been discussed in our paper. Same as Mopro, the key idea of [R2] is leveraging multiple prototypes to generate  pseudo labels for label noise learning. Our work is tailored for the semi-supervised learning based LNL framework. Our motivation is to solve the widely-ignored class-agnostic loss distribution modeling problem in label noise recognition.

(2) **Different in the use of prototypes**. Same as most methods[R3,R4], [R2] utilize  prototypes to generate pseudo labels to correct noisy labels. In our method, we utilize prototypes for mislabeled sample recognition.

(3) **Different in the learning of prototypes**.  Our method utilizes a **different optimizing objective** for prototypes from [R2]. In our method, the prototypes are learnt via an EM style iterative framework, where the latent variable in EM indicates the sample to be clean or not clean. Updating the prototypes, our method converges to a data partition effectively dividing clean and noise data. In the iterative framework of [R2], the method is supposed to converge to correct labels for training samples. Besides, our method utilizes a **different optimizing method** from [R2]. Different from most methods[R3,R4] that utilize prototypical contrastive objective for end-to-end prototype learning, [R2] utilizes a clustering strategy and selects prototypes from randomly sampled training data in each epoch. In our method, our prototypes are also end-to-end learnable from the whole dataset as [R3,R4]. Additionally, the learning of prototypes in our method further takes advantage of "small loss prior".

Moreover, our method achieves 75.4 acc on Clothing1m, while the result of [R2] is 74.45  (see Table.1 in [R2], 1M noisy setting). It suggests that our method outperforms [R2].

We also notice that  [R2] proposes an interesting idea of utilizing multiple prototypes for a single class so as to better model intra-class data distribution. The idea is potentially beneficial to our method, and we will discuss [R2] in our final version of paper.

[R2] Han et.al. "Deep self-learning from noisy labels." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF international conference on computer vision. 2019. https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCV_2019/papers/Han_Deep_Self-Learning_From_Noisy_Labels_ICCV_2019_paper.pdf.

[R3] Li et.al. "MoPro: Webly Supervised Learning with Momentum Prototypes." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020.

[R4] Junnan et.al. "Learning from noisy data with robust representation learning." In ICCV,pp.9485–9494, 2021

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper presents the work on learning with noisy labels. The core idea of this paper is to strengthen previous the class-agnostic sample selection approach with class prototypes. Moreover, based on a prior framework, this paper shows that the strengthened sample selection approach can improve the cutting-edge performance of state-of-the-art methods effectively.

The strengths of this paper are mainly reflected in promising experimental results. In a series of experimental cases, compared with previous work, the proposed algorithm enjoys outstanding empirical performance. The weaknesses of this paper are reflected in (1) The contributions of this paper are unclear. Specifically, the paper argues that the introduction of class prototypes into sample selection contributes to the research community. However, reviewers consider that the paper somewhat overclaimed its contributions and miss the discussions about related literature. (2) The theoretical analysis did not give a good indication of the effectiveness of the method. 

In the internal discussion between AC and reviewers, all reviewers appreciate that this paper produces solid experimental results. Nevertheless, to make a stronger submission for publication, AC and reviewers unanimously consider that this paper should be enhanced by clarifying/highlighting its novelty, contributions, and revising its theoretical section. Therefore, the recommendation now is "reject".
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score:
This paper provides a potential perspective to handle noisy labels. Empirical results are provided to support its claims. Before rebuttal, reviewers raise several concerns about this paper. The authors provide responses to them.

The responses address partial concerns. However, reviewers still think that this paper cannot reach the acceptance line, particularly due to the lack of discussions about important related work and the theoretical analysis that needs to be revised carefully. Minor modifications are not enough for acceptance. Therefore, the recommendation is "reject".
